title: Staggered Reservation Flex Model and Utilization Scenarios
body:
Purpose:
This working sheet explores a staggered/reserved-commit strategy for Dedicated GPU pools intended to: reduce cash drag from large up-front commits, smooth utilization across seasonal demand, and create predictable price breakpoints for customers that ramp over time. The goal is a set of concrete commit templates (3-phase, 6-phase, and rolling-month) plus a sensitivity view showing unit cost per token/GPU-hour under realistic churn and burst scenarios.

Context + why different from flat commits:
- Many customers balk at large annual commitments (12mo full-burn) due to product/usage uncertainty.
- We can offer staggered starts and smaller initial tranches which trigger discounts as the customer adds subsequent tranches.
- This allows better amortization of provisioning (we can right-size initial pools) while still locking predictable revenue.

Key assumptions (base case):
- GPU type: A100-80GB equiv. Use normalized GPU-hour cost "raw-cloud" = $4.50/hr to Redwood (provisioned infra + infra ops).
- Baseline hosted on-demand price (internal) = $X (not shown here), primary metric = effective $/GPU-hour after commit credits.
- Typical utilization range across customers: 20% (idle-light) to 75% (steady-production).
- Burst tolerance: 20% of peak traffic can be serviced by burst capacity (preemptible/pool) at 30% lower cost to Redwood but with no SLA.
- Commitment term windows: 6m, 12m, 24m. Staggered tranches can be monthly or quarterly.

Model parameters (inputs you can toggle):
- tranche_count (int): 2, 3, 6
- tranche_size_pct (list): % of total commit applied at each tranche. Example 3-tranche: [40, 30, 30]
- tranche_spacing_months (int): 1, 3, 6
- price_break_schedule (list): discounts applied when tranche_n is activated. E.g., [0%, 8%, 15%] meaning 8% off when tranche 2 starts, 15% when tranche 3 starts (applies to committed hours going forward).
- churn_risk_pct (annualized): 10% base (probability customer reduces commit or reneges on renewal)
- utilization_profile (list months): month-by-month expected utilization by tranche activation (example below)

Example scenario (3-phase, quarterly spacing):
Inputs:
- total_reserved_gpus_target = 100 GPUs
- tranche_count = 3
- tranche_size_pct = [30, 35, 35] => 30 GPUs month0, +35 month3 => cumulative 65, +35 month6 => 100
- tranche_spacing_months = 3
- base_commit_price_pct_discount = [0%, 7%, 13%] applied to committed-hour baseline price
- expected utilization on committed pool by active GPUs: month0-month2 = 50% of provisioned, month3-month5 = 62%, month6+ = 70%

Quick arithmetic (simplified):
- Raw cost (Redwood) per hour per GPU = $4.50 => monthly cost per GPU (720h) = $3,240
- Committed discount pass-through assumption: we price customer such that effective $/GPU-hr after their discount = raw_cost * (1 - discount) * markup_factor. For this exercise markup_factor=1.15 (target margin on committed hours)
- Month0: provision 30 GPUs => monthly cost = 30 * 3240 = $97,200. Effective billed rate per GPU after 0% discount = 4.50 * 1.15 = $5.175/hr => revenue if fully utilized = 30 * 720 * 5.175 = $111,780. But at 50% utilization realized revenue = $55,890. Effective unit revenue per utilized GPU-hour = $5.175 (billing), but fixed provisioning causes unit economics to worsen when utilization low.
- Month3 addition: +35 GPUs, new cumulative discounts apply to all committed GPUs per schedule (we assume discount tier applies retroactively to all committed hours from activation month onward). This lowers per-hour customer price and shifts margin.

Observations from the numeric example:
- Front-loading risk: Early months show large negative margin vs provisioned cost if utilization < ~60% depending on discount schedule and markup.
- Gradual ramp reduces peak idle capacity and matches customer growth profile, but discount retroactivity reduces per-hour realized margin on early tranches once later tranches hit (tradeoff).
- Non-retroactive discount variant: apply discount only to newly added tranche capacity (not to previously committed GPUs). That preserves early-margin but complicates billing and revenue recognition.

Comparison of billing policies (qualitative):
1) Retroactive tier discount (simple for customer, simple marketing): when tier N triggers, discount applies to whole commit. Pros: easy to explain; consistent unit price for the account. Cons: backend accounting churn; early tranche margin erosion.
2) Non-retroactive tranche pricing: each tranche billed at the discount in effect when the tranche was purchased. Pros: preserves margin on early tranches. Cons: more complex invoices; customers may prefer single blended rate.
3) Hybrid rolling credit: issue a one-time credit when the next tranche hits to reimburse early customers for earlier overcharges (booked as credit). Medium complexity.

Sensitivity checks to run in spreadsheet (these should be separate tabs):
- Sensitivity: utilization +/- 10/20/30%
- Sensitivity: churn risk (0%, 10%, 25%) with assumptions on how much reserved capacity is left idle until re-sold or scaled down (lead time to scale = 3 months)
- Sensitivity: burst mix (0%, 10%, 20% served by preemptible) and preemptible price/cost differential
- Sensitivity: retroactive vs non-retroactive discounting on NPV of committed revenue over term

Proposed commit templates (customer-facing product options):
A) Phased Ramp Quarterly (3-tranche) - marketing name: "Ramp & Save"
- Term: 12 months
- Tranches: 30/35/35% at months 0/3/6
- Discount milestones: 0% / 7% / 13% applied retroactively
- Use-case: customers with clear roadmap and expected Q-o-Q growth
- Redwood internal note: requires billing system support for retro discounts and forecasting window to provision GPUs by month N-1

B) Monthly Rolling Reserve (6-tranche) - "Stepped Commit"
- Term: 12 months
- Tranches: equal 16.66% monthly additions for first 6 months
- Discount milestones: 0 / 4% / 6% / 8% / 10% / 12% (applied non-retroactively to keep early margins)
- Use-case: customers with month-over-month growth and high uncertainty
- Redwood internal note: more complex accounting but smoother operational provisioning

C) Anchor + Top-up (2-tranche hybrid) - "Anchor + Burst"
- Term: 12 or 24 months
- Tranches: anchor 60% up-front, top-up 40% at month 6
- Discount: 0% -> 10% (retroactive to full commit) with option for customers to choose non-retro pricing to get slightly higher per-hour price but simpler billing
- Use-case: enterprise customers who need a base guarantee plus growth option

Operational considerations (SRE/Capacity):
- Provision lead time: scheduling GPUs into pools has 4-6 weeks lead time to avoid allocation shortages during tranche months. Need provisioning calendar tied to billing triggers.
- Pool fragmentation: staggered trims can create many small pools — run a consolidation policy to co-locate same account tranches onto same pool to increase pack utilization.
- Autoscaling: tranche activation should notify autoscaling policies to attach warm nodes to pool before billing cycle begins (avoid SLA gap).

Revenue recognition / finance notes:
- Retroactive discounts require clear accounting treatment for revenue deferral/credits. Finance needs a template for booking one-time credits and impact on churn ARR forecasting.
- Non-retroactive keeps simpler revenue per tranche, easier to forecast. Consider defaulting to non-retroactive for smaller customers and offering retroactive as an upsell/negotiated term.

Customer UX draft language (to include on pricing page):
"Start small and grow into deeper discounts. Choose a phased reservation plan that matches your traffic profile — as you add subsequent tranches, you'll unlock deeper committed pricing. We provide clear invoices showing each tranche and crediting if you opt into the retroactive discount."

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to model failed tranche activations when customer never purchases tranche N? (current spreadsheet assumes they do; add probability tree for partial completion)
- Need to run cohort-level analysis on historical customers (past 24 months) to estimate realistic tranche completion rates and ramp curves. Ask solutions-eng for data. (Owner: Jamal Rivera)
- Billing system feasibility: can we implement retroactive discounting cleanly? (Owner: Liam O'Connor to sync with billing infra)
- SLA for burst: define explicit SLA boundaries (what constitutes allowed preemptible fallback) and how customer-facing SLAs change during ramp months. (Owner: SRE)

Next steps (action items):
- Convert scenario text into a multi-tab spreadsheet with: inputs, monthly cashflow by tranche, sensitivity engine, and NPV/revenue-recognition tab. (Priya)
- Run cohort analysis for tranche completion rates and attach as data-driven priors (Jamal)
- Productize one template (likely Phased Ramp Quarterly) as beta offering for 3 pilot customers; track utilization and invoice complexity. (PM + Sales)

Quick sketch of spreadsheet tab layout (for whoever is building it):
1_inputs: toggle GPUs, tranche_schedule, discounts, utilization curves, churn
2_monthly_provisioning: month rows, GPUs provisioned, active tranches, cumulative GPUs, raw cost, billed rev, net margin
3_sensitivity: scenario toggles and output dashboards (unit $/GPU-hr, pool idle %, margin)
4_cohort_priors: historic ramp examples, percent completing tranche 2/3, median time to top-up
5_finance_offsets: credit booking schedule, revenue deferral examples, journal entry mockups
6_operational_notes: provisioning calendar, pool labels, autoscaler hooks

Notes-to-self (quick):
- Keep retro discounts optional per account; default non-retro for self-serve UI to reduce ops complexity.
- Flag: if we offer retro discounts for >500 GPU commits, we should require 24mo notice to avoid revenue whipsaw.
